entities.summary:
Stephanus Brodericus, known as Stjepan Brodarić, was a pivotal Croatian-Hungarian bishop, diplomat, chancellor, and humanist writer whose career spanned the tumultuous period leading up to and immediately following the catastrophic Battle of Mohács in 1526. Born into a noble Croatian family, his life exemplified the intersection of ecclesiastical power, political service, and intellectual pursuits characteristic of the late medieval and early modern Central European elite. His enduring significance lies not only in his active participation in the highest echelons of Hungarian governance but also in his singular role as a chronicler of one of Europe's most decisive military defeats.

Brodarić’s intellectual formation began at the University of Pécs, a hub of humanist learning, before he pursued advanced studies in Italy, receiving his Doctorate in Canon Law from the University of Padua in 1506. His rapid ascent in the ecclesiastical hierarchy saw him become Bishop of Sirmio (Syrmia) by 1513, a strategically important diocese on the Ottoman frontier, and eventually Bishop of Pécs in 1537. Concurrently, he served as a trusted advisor and diplomat for King Louis II of Hungary, rising to the influential position of Royal Chancellor. His diplomatic missions often involved navigating the complex political landscape of Central Europe, dealing with both internal Hungarian factions and external threats, primarily the burgeoning Ottoman Empire.

entities.summary:
Stjepan Brodarić, known in Latin as Stephanus Brodericus, was a pivotal Croatian-Hungarian bishop, diplomat, and humanist writer whose career unfolded during the tumultuous early 16th century, a period defined by the relentless advance of the Ottoman Empire into Central Europe. Born in Herešin in 1480, his intellectual prowess led him through the esteemed universities of Pécs, Bologna, and Padua, culminating in a Doctorate in Canon Law in 1506. His unique position as Chancellor of King Louis II of Hungary and an eyewitness to the catastrophic Battle of Mohács in 1526 solidified his significance as a chronicler of one of the most devastating defeats in Hungarian history.

Brodarić's professional trajectory was marked by rapid ascent within both ecclesiastical and political spheres. Following his legal studies, he served as a canon in Pécs and Zagreb before undertaking significant diplomatic missions for the Hungarian crown. He became Bishop of Sirmio in 1521, and later Bishop of Vác, while concurrently holding the influential position of Royal Chancellor. His diplomatic acumen was deployed in efforts to forge alliances against the Ottomans, though ultimately to no avail. His most enduring contribution, however, stems from his direct involvement and subsequent detailed account of the Battle of Mohács, where the Hungarian forces suffered a crushing defeat and King Louis II perished.
